literature.lead_zh: 本期尼帕病毒研究集中呈现以下进展。
key_findings_zh: 这些最小蛋白的寡聚形式相较于其单体构建单元表现出增强的效力,并且提高了逃逸突变体出现的障碍。 [10.64898/2026.09.14.751546]
通过腹腔途径接种使用103 TCID50感染剂量在两种菌株中均导致了一致且严重的疾病。相比之下,动物通过鼻腔途径接种10 TCID50剂量时更容易感染,且导致了均匀的致死率。 [10.3390/v18091030]

该研究报道,qPCR已被验证可用于兽医诊断中快速且可靠地检测尼帕病毒及其他病原体。 [10.1201/9781003459521-2]

papers.title: Computational design of potent, broadly neutralizing anti-Nipah virus and Hendra virus miniproteins
papers.abstract: Abstract The prototype members of the genus Henipavirus, Nipah virus (NiV) and Hendra virus (HeV), cause recurrent zoonotic spillovers with case fatality rates ranging from 40-90% in humans. Currently, there are no approved vaccines or therapeutics for use in humans. Neutralizing antibodies targeting the NiV/HeV F-or G-glycoproteins protect animals from lethal challenge and are a main correlate of protection. However, antibody-based formulations are expensive, typically requiring hospital admission for administration and cold-chain for storage and transportation. To address the lack of shelf-stable clinical countermeasures, we computationally designed thermostable miniproteins that cross-react with subnanomolar affinities with both NiV and HeV F and G glycoproteins and inhibit viral entry in vitro with potencies comparable to lead antibodies. Oligomerized forms of these miniproteins have enhanced potency relative to their monomeric building blocks and increase the barrier for emergence of escape mutants, establishing them as promising preclinical candidates against these deadly viruses.

papers.title: Defining Challenge Conditions for Nipah Virus in the Syrian Golden Hamster Model: Effects of Dose, Exposure Route and Viral Strain
papers.abstract: Nipah virus (NiV) is a highly pathogenic zoonotic virus for which no licensed vaccines or therapeutics are currently available, necessitating well-characterised animal models to support countermeasure development. This study aimed to establish an appropriate challenge dose in the Syrian golden hamster model at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), incorporating both intraperitoneal (i.p.) and intranasal (i.n.) routes of infection and two clinically relevant strains, NiV-Malaysia (NiV-M) and NiV-Bangladesh (NiV-B). Due to a different challenge doses and susceptibilities of hamsters to NiV being reported in the literature, there is a prerequisite to define the model parameters upon establishment in a new facility. Dose-ranging studies were performed across multiple independent experiments assessing survival, clinical progression and histopathological outcomes. Challenge via the i.p. route produced consistent and severe disease using an infectious dose of 103 TCID50 for both strains. In contrast, animals were more susceptible to infection via i.n. challenge with a dose of 10 TCID50 resulting in uniform lethality. For both challenge routes, respiratory and neurological disease manifestations were observed. These distinct disease phenotypes were supported by histopathological findings and viral RNA distribution in affected organs. Differences between strains were evident, with NiV-B showing a tendency towards a broader pulmonary pathology at lower doses after i.n. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that challenge dose, route of exposure, and viral strain influence disease outcomes in the hamster model.

papers.title_zh: 在叙利亚金hamster模型中定义尼帕病毒(尼帕病毒)的挑战条件:剂量、暴露途径和病毒株的影响
papers.source_body_en: Nipah virus (NiV) is a highly pathogenic zoonotic virus for which no licensed vaccines or therapeutics are currently available, necessitating well-characterised animal models to support countermeasure development. This study aimed to establish an appropriate challenge dose in the Syrian golden hamster model at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), incorporating both intraperitoneal (i.p.) and intranasal (i.n.) routes of infection and two clinically relevant strains, NiV-Malaysia (NiV-M) and NiV-Bangladesh (NiV-B). Due to a different challenge doses and susceptibilities of hamsters to NiV being reported in the literature, there is a prerequisite to define the model parameters upon establishment in a new facility. Dose-ranging studies were performed across multiple independent experiments assessing survival, clinical progression and histopathological outcomes. Challenge via the i.p. route produced consistent and severe disease using an infectious dose of 103 TCID50 for both strains. In contrast, animals were more susceptible to infection via i.n. challenge with a dose of 10 TCID50 resulting in uniform lethality. For both challenge routes, respiratory and neurological disease manifestations were observed. These distinct disease phenotypes were supported by histopathological findings and viral RNA distribution in affected organs. Differences between strains were evident, with NiV-B showing a tendency towards a broader pulmonary pathology at lower doses after i.n. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that challenge dose, route of exposure, and viral strain influence disease outcomes in the hamster model.
papers.abstract_zh: 尼帕病毒(NiV)是一种高致病性的人兽共患病病毒,目前尚无获批的疫苗或治疗药物,因此需要建立良好的动物模型以支持对策的开发。本研究旨在确定英国卫生安全局(UKHSA)叙利亚金hamster模型中的适当感染剂量,包括腹腔(i.p.)和鼻腔(i.n.)两种感染途径,以及两种具有临床相关性的NiV毒株,即NiV-Malaysia(NiV-M)和NiV-Bangladesh(NiV-B)。由于文献中报道了hamster对NiV的不同感染剂量和易感性,因此在新设施中建立模型时,有必要定义模型参数。通过多个独立实验评估存活率、临床进展和组织病理学结果,进行了剂量范围研究。通过腹腔途径感染使用103 TCID50的感染剂量,两种毒株均表现出一致且严重的疾病。相比之下,通过鼻腔途径感染时,使用10 TCID50的剂量导致动物更容易感染,并且表现出统一的致死性。对于两种感染途径,均观察到呼吸系统和神经系统疾病的表现。这些不同的疾病表型得到了受影响器官中组织病理学发现和病毒RNA分布的支持。毒株之间存在差异,NiV-B在较低剂量下通过鼻腔途径感染时表现出更广泛的肺部病理变化。总体而言,这些发现表明,在hamster模型中,感染剂量、暴露途径和病毒毒株会影响疾病结果。

Indian J Med Res. doi: 10.25259/ IJMR_3319_2026 Emerging and re-emerging viral infections have repeatedly tested India's capacity for rapid diagnosis, surveillance and outbreak response. Over the past decade, the COVID-19 pandemic and outbreaks of Nipah virus disease, Zika virus infection, Chandipura virus and other vector-borne and zoonotic infections have shown that preparedness depends not only on scientific discovery, but on the ability to translate laboratory evidence into deployable diagnostics, surveillance systems and timely public-health action. Established in 1952 as the Virus Research Centre and renamed the National Institute of Virology (NIV) in 1978, ICMR–NIV, Pune, has evolved into India's premier virology institute, integrating basic research with the development of medical countermeasures, outbreak investigation and pandemic preparedness. Over the past decade, its research and scientific capabilities have contributed across this continuum from diagnostic preparedness and genomic surveillance to field-based outbreak response and the detection of emerging viral threats. It serves as the national resource centre for a network of 167 Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) and 23 biosafety level-3 laboratories, and maintains a national repository of authenticated virus strains supporting the indigenous development of diagnostics, vaccines and therapeutics (Box). This article examines key examples from the past decade illustrating how sustained virological research and institutional capacity have supported public-health action during outbreaks while strengthening national preparedness. Building pandemic preparedness: from diagnostic science to a national response: The early COVID-19 pandemic tested whether pre-existing scientific capacity could be rapidly converted into a population- level response. India required validated diagnostic protocols, quality-assured testing and mechanisms for expanding laboratory capacity across a geographically diverse country. NIV supported standardisation of molecular testing across the VRDL network; indigenous in vitro-transcribed RNA controls provided a positive-control resource when access to such material was constrained.1,2 National laboratory surveillance expanded from around 250 tests per day in early March 2020 to 50,000 per day by end-April, with 99% of districts reporting testing by then,3 a national, multi- institutional achievement to which NIV's reference- laboratory functions contributed. NIV also drove the shift from diagnosis to molecular epidemiology and countermeasure development. Sequencing and isolation of the first SARS-CoV-2 viruses from India supported further research on diagnostics, antivirals and vaccines,4,5 while genomic surveillance characterised the B.1.617 lineage and key spike mutations during Maharashtra's second wave.6 The Institute also contributed to the development of indigenous vaccines, including the inactivated vaccine Covaxin,7,8 and the world's first approved DNA vaccine against SARS-CoV-2, and has continuously tracked emerging variants and vaccine-induced immune responses to inform booster-dose policy. A complementary translational effort saw NIV develop an indigenous IgG-based antibody assay for past SARS- CoV-2 infection, transfer the technology to industry and validate it for field use — enabling the serosurveillance studies that helped inform containment and mitigation strategy across the country.9-11 Together, these contributions illustrate a continuum from standardised 2 INDIAN J MED RES, MONTH 2026 testing and diagnostic scale-up to genomic intelligence and indigenous countermeasure development and how laboratory research can become embedded in systems for epidemic response and public-health decision-making. Responding to high-consequence zoonoses: The Nipah experience: If COVID-19 demonstrated the importance of scale, Nipah virus disease has repeatedly demonstrated the importance of speed. Across outbreaks in Kerala and West Bengal since 2018, NIV teams have combined rapid laboratory confirmation with serosurveillance of contacts and surveillance of Pteropus bat populations, extending the response beyond human case confirmation to the animal–human interface.12,13 A field laboratory established during the earliest outbreaks gave way, from 2023 onward, to a rapidly deployable mobile BSL-3 laboratory that enabled onsite diagnosis within approximately four hours during the Kozhikode outbreak.14 This capability in high-containment science and field deployment also positions NIV to strengthen national multisectoral preparedness through structured One Health mock drills such as ‘Vishanu Yuddh Abhyas’- the 2024 edition of which demonstrated the value of coordinating human-health, animal-husbandry and wildlife sectors around a simulated zoonotic outbreak with regular NIV participation in such exercises identified as a priority for strengthening interagency coordination. The significance lies not simply in faster diagnosis, but in shortening the interval between suspicion and actionable evidence and how reference- laboratory expertise can evolve into a more distributed, multisectoral preparedness model. Adapting surveillance to emerging and re-emerging threats: NIV's surveillance has repeatedly adapted to shifting viral and vector ecologies. Expanded Zika screening identified infections in newer geographical settings, as well as dengue–chikungunya co- infections. The 2024 Pune outbreak reflected this, integrating molecular, epidemiological and genomic characterisation.15,16 A decade of chikungunya serosurveillance in Pune documented rising population exposure, while genomic studies tracked viral resurgence and evolution.17,18 For Kyasanur Forest disease (KFD), phylogeographic analysis traced spread beyond its historical focus into Sindhudurg district of Maharashtra, prompting state action on vaccinating high-risk forest and health workers.19,20 A multicentre field evaluation showed high performance for a portable point-of-care assay.21 An adjuvant whole-virion vaccine candidate developed with Indian Immunologicals Ltd has now completed preclinical safety and efficacy evaluation.22 Sustained VRDL-based surveillance for respiratory illness also functioned as a sentinel for zoonotic spillover. In 2024, a routine sample led to confirmation of India's second human case of avian influenza A(H9N2), with genomic characterisation and antiviral- susceptibility testing informing risk assessment.23 NIV has similarly identified and characterised outbreaks of Chandipura virus, including India's largest, in Gujarat in 2024,24 and the aetiological agents behind India's largest Guillain-Barré syndrome outbreak, contributing directly to outbreak containment.25 Diagnostic development also kept pace with newly emerging global threats: indigenous IgM/IgG ELISAs for mpox virus extended national testing capacity for this newly emerging orthopoxvirus.26 Together, these examples show how NIV's surveillance has evolved from confirming known threats to detecting the unexpected, serology tracking population exposure, genomics tracing viral spread, and routine networks doubling as sentinels for emerging pathogens. Beyond outbreak response: national systems and self- reliance: Much of NIV's public-health value lies in infrastructure sustained between emergencies. Over the past decade, it has trained more than 6,000 personnel from VRDL laboratories nationwide and produced and supplied nearly 1.24 lakh MAC-ELISA kits for dengue, chikungunya and Japanese encephalitis to national surveillance programmes. Its Mumbai Unit is one of only seven WHO Global Specialised Laboratories for polio worldwide and the only one in a developing country. The Unit sustains Acute Flaccid Paralysis and environmental surveillance, and established India's iVDPV surveillance network, a global first. It also serves as the WHO Regional Reference Laboratory for measles and rubella for South-East Asia, having supported expansion of the regional network from 12 to 28 accredited laboratories. Beyond surveillance, the Institute's virus repository supplied 27 authenticated strains to 18 institutions in 2025–26 alone, while a growing portfolio of technologies and patents spanning multiplex diagnostic assays, novel antivirals and vaccine candidates continues to move toward industry transfer and licensing. Together, these functions have strengthened India's self-reliance in biomedical research well beyond any single outbreak response. From episodic response to durable preparedness: Different threats have demanded different capabilities: COVID-19 required scale and decentralisation; 3 TANWAR: FROM RESEARCH TO IMPACT Nipah required speed and proximity; arboviral and zoonotic threats required surveillance responsive to shifting epidemiology; and sustained networks proved essential for recognising the unexpected. National responses inevitably depend on the combined efforts of governments, laboratories, clinicians and communities. Even so, NIV's trajectory over the past decade illustrates how sustained investment in reference diagnostics, laboratory networks, genomics, high-containment science and field investigation generates value that extends well beyond individual publications — strengthening the systems through which India detects, interprets and responds to emerging viral threats. Looking ahead — director's perspective: ‘Over the next five years, ICMR–NIV will prioritise the development of indigenous medical countermeasures, including antiviral therapeutics, next-generation vaccine platforms, monoclonal antibodies, and rapid, affordable diagnostics, while advancing fundamental virology to deepen understanding of virus–host interactions, viral evolution, pathogenesis, and protective immune responses. Emerging opportunities in genomics, artificial intelligence, advanced disease modelling, and integrated One Health surveillance will support the early detection and effective control of emerging infections. The Institute will further strengthen biorepositories, high-containment laboratory capacity, and scientific training through strategic partnerships with academia, industry, and public-health agencies. By providing scientific leadership and coordinating the Zonal NIV network, ICMR–NIV will accelerate innovation and strengthen India’s preparedness and response to future outbreaks and pandemics.’ (Dr Naveen Kumar, Director, ICMR–National Institute of Virology, Pune) Financial support and sponsorship: None. papers.title: Validation and Standardization of PCR Analysis in Veterinary Disease Diagnosis
papers.abstract: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a fundamental technique in molecular biology that enables the exponential amplification of specific DNA sequences with exceptional sensitivity and precision. Since its development, PCR has become indispensable in research, clinical diagnostics, and veterinary medicine. The advent of real-time PCR, also known as quantitative PCR (qPCR), has further transformed molecular diagnostics by allowing the simultaneous amplification and real-time detection of nucleic acids through fluorescence-based chemistries. Unlike conventional PCR, which requires post-amplification analysis such as agarose gel electrophoresis, qPCR integrates detection into the amplification process, significantly reducing contamination risks, improving accuracy, and shortening turnaround time. Numerous PCR variants have expanded its scope and versatility. Techniques such as multiplex-PCR enable the simultaneous detection of multiple targets, while nested PCR enhances sensitivity and specificity. Other adaptations, including RAPD-PCR, AFLP-PCR, RFLP-PCR, and colony PCR, are widely applied in pathogen identification, population genetics, phylogenetic studies, and the analysis of genetic diversity. In veterinary diagnostics, qPCR has been validated for the rapid and reliable detection of important pathogens, including Jaagsiekte sheep retrovirus (JSRV), Zika virus, Nipah virus, bovine viral agents, and Pasteurella multocida in swine, supporting effective disease surveillance and control programs. Although PCR faces limitations such as contamination risks, primer design complexity, and dependence on specialized equipment, ongoing advancements – including nanoparticle-assisted PCR, automation, and AI-driven data analysis – are improving robustness, throughput, and interpretative power. Collectively, PCR and its advanced formats continue to revolutionize molecular diagnostics by enhancing sensitivity, efficiency, and disease-monitoring capabilities.
